title: Navigating Optimization and Security Challenges in the AI-Driven Digital Economy: From Classical Limits to Quantum Solutions
journal_or_venue: International Conference on AI and the Digital Economy (CADE 2025)
abstract_summary: This paper examines how emerging quantum computing paradigms can address optimization bottlenecks and security vulnerabilities in the AI-driven digital economy. It focuses on the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and quantum-state-based cryptographic protocols (e.g., QDS), proposing a hybrid quantum-classical architecture suitable for NISQ devices and comparing classical, post-quantum, and quantum approaches across industry use cases.
methodology_description: This paper employs a conceptual and synthesis-based methodology rather than reporting new empirical experiments. The authors perform a state-of-the-art literature review to identify key optimization and security challenges in AI-driven digital-economy domains (finance, logistics, healthcare, smart cities, etc.). They introduce and analyze two quantum paradigms (the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for combinatorial/QUBO optimization and quantum-state-based cryptographic protocols such as Quantum Digital Signatures (QDS) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for secure communications). Building on the literature, the paper proposes a Hybrid Quantum–Classical Architecture (HQCA) that integrates quantum subroutines into classical AI workflows via a variational feedback loop (classical preprocessing → quantum subroutine → classical postprocessing). The methodology includes an algorithmic description (pseudo-code, Algorithm 1) of the HQCA loop, a description of mapping optimization problems to QUBO/Hamiltonian form, and specification of the QAOA variational state and parameter update cycle using classical optimizers (e.g., COBYLA, SPSA, Bayesian optimization). For the security module, the methodology describes attaching quantum signatures to model updates and verifying them via fidelity/swap tests or trace-distance thresholds. Finally, the authors perform comparative, qualitative analyses (tables comparing classical vs QAOA optimization, classical vs PQC vs QSBC security models, and sector readiness/use-case mapping) and discuss feasibility and integration considerations referencing existing cloud-accessible hardware and middleware (Qiskit, Cirq, Amazon Braket, PennyLane) and prior proof-of-concept results from the literature.
key_findings: [supported] Classical optimization techniques struggle with large-scale combinatorial and non-convex problems encountered in AI-driven finance, logistics, and smart-city applications.
[supported] AI systems face significant security and privacy risks (model theft, adversarial attacks, data leakage) that threaten reliability and trust in sensitive domains.
[supported] Classical public-key schemes (e.g., RSA, ECC) are vulnerable to future quantum attacks, motivating transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
[supported] NISQ-era hardware (IBM, IonQ, D-Wave) and cloud middleware (Qiskit, Cirq, Amazon Braket, PennyLane) enable hybrid quantum-classical workflows today.
[supported] Current quantum hardware remains limited by noise, decoherence, and low logical qubit counts, constraining fully quantum solutions.

[speculative] The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a promising variational approach for QUBO-style combinatorial optimization relevant to financial portfolio optimization and logistics.

[speculative] Hybrid quantum-classical architectures (HQCA) that offload target subroutines (e.g., QAOA) to QPUs while retaining classical orchestration are a practical near-term deployment strategy.

[speculative] Quantum-state-based cryptographic protocols (e.g., Quantum Digital Signatures, QKD-style encryption) can provide physics-rooted properties (no-cloning, measurement collapse) that improve authentication and tamper-detection in distributed AI systems.
[supported] Experimental QDS testbeds have been demonstrated for long-distance message authentication (the paper cites authentication of ~10 kB messages over ~50 km fibre links).

[supported] NIST-selected post-quantum algorithms (e.g., Kyber, Dilithium, SPHINCS+) provide deployable PQC options and are compatible with hybrid stacks that combine PQC for classical channels with quantum protocols for sensitive loops.
[speculative] Sector readiness varies: finance and logistics show higher near-term feasibility for HQCA pilots, whereas healthcare and manufacturing face more infrastructure and regulatory barriers.
[supported] Middleware and cloud hybrid APIs (Qiskit Runtime, Amazon Braket Hybrid Jobs) lower integration complexity by enabling classical applications to offload quantum subroutines.
results_summary: The paper argues that the twin challenges of combinatorial optimization and security in AI-driven financial and related services can be meaningfully addressed by hybrid quantum-classical approaches. It promotes QAOA for targeted combinatorial tasks and quantum-state-based cryptographic protocols (e.g., QDS/QKD) for enhanced authentication and confidentiality. While acknowledging NISQ hardware limitations (noise, limited qubit counts), the authors present HQCA as an iterative variational loop where quantum modules augment classical pipelines. They cite small-scale proof-of-concept results and existing cloud/middleware ecosystems that demonstrate feasibility for constrained use cases (notably finance and logistics), but emphasize that broad quantum advantage and large-scale deployment remain subject to hardware maturation, noise mitigation, and standardization.

The advantage is therefore positioned as promising and partially evidenced in limited experiments, but still speculative for broad, practical financial-services deployment given current NISQ hardware constraints and lack of large-scale demonstrations.
